title: Greenland sharks live for centuries and may not mature until about 150
body: Greenland sharks drift through cold Arctic and North Atlantic water at about 0.34 metres per second and grow only half a centimetre to a centimetre a year. In 2016, researchers estimated their ages by **radiocarbon dating crystals in the sharks’ eye lenses**. The species lives at least 272 years, and the oldest individual came out at 392 years, give or take 120, which makes it the longest-lived vertebrate known. Living that slowly has a cost: the sharks are thought to reach sexual maturity only at around 150 years of age.

slides.label: years: the estimated age of the oldest Greenland shark in a 2016 study
slides.text: Even the low end of that range, 272 years, beats every other vertebrate known.

slides.heading: A Greenland shark’s life next to a human one
slides.note: Jeanne Calment lived 122 years; the oldest shark’s age was estimated at 392 ± 120

slides.question: How long was the largest confirmed Greenland shark?
slides.explanation: The largest confirmed specimen measured 6.4 m and weighed around 1,023 kg. Most adults are 4 to 5 m long.

slides.heading: Life in the slow lane
items: Grows about 0.5 to 1 cm a year
Cruises at about 0.34 metres per second, slower than a strolling person
Reaches sexual maturity at around 150 years
Adults are 4 to 5 m long; the largest confirmed measured 6.4 m

slides.question: How did the 2016 study work out the sharks’ ages?
options: Radiocarbon dating of the eye lens
slides.explanation: Crystals in the eye lens were radiocarbon dated, giving an estimated lifespan of at least 272 years.
